'''''Berberis thunbergii''''', the '''Japanese barberry''', '''Thunberg's barberry''', or '''red barberry''',<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.djroger.com/red_barberry.htm|title=Moonshine Designs Nursery|access-date=2008-03-29|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080402030416/http://www.djroger.com/red_barberry.htm|archive-date=2 April 2008}}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the barberry family Berberidaceae, [[native plant|native]] to Japan and eastern Asia, though widely naturalized in China and North America, where it has become a problematic invasive in many places, leading to declines in species diversity, increased tick habitat, and soil changes.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=233500242|title=''Berberis thunbergii'' in Flora of China @ efloras.org|website=efloras.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=233500242|title=''Berberis thunbergii'' in Flora of North America @ efloras.org|website=efloras.org}}</ref><ref name=nps>{{cite web
  | first = Jil M.
  | last = Swearingen
  | title = Least Wanted: Japanese Barberry
  | publisher = U.S. National Park Service
  | url = http://www.nps.gov/plants/alien/fact/beth1.htm
  | url-status = dead
  | date = 7 July 2009
  | access-date = 20 March 2011
  | archive-date = 14 May 2011
  | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110514131751/http://www.nps.gov/plants/alien/fact/beth1.htm
  }}</ref> Growing to {{convert|1|m|ftin|abbr=on}} tall by {{convert|2.5|m|ftin|abbr=on}} broad, it is a small [[deciduous]] shrub with green leaves turning red in the autumn, brilliant red fruits in autumn and pale yellow flowers in spring.<ref name=AZEGP>{{cite book
| editor-last = Brickell
| editor-first = Christopher
| title = The Royal Horticultural Society A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants
| year = 2008
| publisher = Dorling Kindersley
| location = United Kingdom
| isbn = 9781405332965}}</ref>

==Description==
''B. thunbergii'' has deeply grooved, brown, spiny branches with a single (occasionally tridentine) spine (actually a highly modified leaf) at each shoot node. The [[leaves]] are green to blue-green (reddish or purple in some horticultural variants), very small, spatula to [[leaf shape|oval shaped]], {{cvt|12–24|mm|frac=16}} long and {{cvt|3–15|mm|frac=16}} broad; they are produced in clusters of 2–6 on a dwarf shoot in the axil of each spine. The [[flower]]s are pale yellow, {{cvt|5–8|mm|frac=32}} diameter, produced in drooping {{cvt|1–1.5|cm|frac=8}} long umbrella-shaped clusters of 2–5; flowering is from mid spring to early summer. The edible fruit is a glossy bright red to orange-red, ovoid [[Berry (botany)|berry]] {{cvt|7–10|mm|frac=32}} long and {{cvt|4–7|mm|frac=32}} broad, containing a single [[seed]]. They mature during late summer and fall and persist through the winter.<ref name=nps />

==Identification==
This species is sometimes confused with ''[[Berberis canadensis]]'' (American barberry), ''[[Berberis vulgaris]]'' (common or European barberry), and other deciduous ''Berberis'' species; it is most readily distinguished by the flowers being produced in [[umbel]]s, not [[raceme]]s.<ref name="MDNR" />

==Cultivation==
[[File:Japanese barberry.jpg|thumb|Berries on an ornamental plant in winter]]

''Berberis thunbergii'' is widely grown as an [[ornamental plant]],<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/2183/berberis-thunbergii/details | title = Berberis thunbergii | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 October 2023}}</ref> both in Japan and elsewhere in the [[temperateness|temperate]] [[Northern Hemisphere]]. [[Berberis cultivar|Numerous cultivar]]s have been selected, including plants selected for yellow, dark red to violet, or [[variegation|variegated]] foliage, erect growth (for [[hedge (gardening)|hedge]] use), and dwarf size. In Brazil, the plant is popularly known as Japanese barberis, and is widely cultivated in hedges and flower beds.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Canales |first1=Claudia |title=Berberis thunbergii: encante seu jardim com a popular Berbére-japonês. |url=https://maniadeplantas.com.br/berberis-thunbergii-popular-berbere-japones/ |language=pt-BR |date=18 April 2024}}</ref>

==Invasive species==
[[File:Berberis thunbergii flowers in Pennwood State Park.jpg|thumb|Flowers in an [[umbel]] on naturalized ''Berberis thunbergii'' in the eastern United States]]
Japanese barberry can be found in most northeastern and [[Great Lakes]] states of the United States and in the eastern Canadian provinces.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Link |first1=Arthur F. |last2=Turnblacer |first2=Trey |last3=Snyder |first3=Cierra K. |last4=Daugherty |first4=Sarah E. |last5=Utz |first5=Ryan M. |date=March 2018 |title=Low Recruitment of Native Trees in a Deciduous Forest Associated with Japanese Barberry ( Berberis thunbergii ) Invasion |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S1939729118000019/type/journal_article |journal=Invasive Plant Science and Management |language=en |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=20–26 |doi=10.1017/inp.2018.1 |issn=1939-7291|url-access=subscription }}</ref> A current map of its distribution can be found at the Early Detection and Distribution Mapping System (EDDmapS).<ref name="EDDMapS">EDDMapS. 2019. Early Detection & Distribution Mapping System. The University of Georgia - Center for Invasive Species and Ecosystem Health. Available online at [https://www.eddmaps.org/distribution/uscounty.cfm?sub=3010 "http://www.eddmaps.org/"]; last accessed 27 October 2019.</ref> In recent years, ''Berberis thunbergii'' has been recognized as an [[invasive species]] in many parts of the eastern United States and Canada.<ref name=nps /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ward |first1=Jeffrey S. |last2=Williams |first2=Scott C. |last3=Worthley |first3=Thomas E. |date=May 2010 |title=Effectiveness of Two-Stage Control Strategies for Japanese Barberry ( Berberis thunbergii ) Varies by Initial Clump Size |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S1939729100001140/type/journal_article |journal=Invasive Plant Science and Management |language=en |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=60–69 |doi=10.1614/IPSM-D-09-00003.1 |issn=1939-7291|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The Plant Conservation Alliance's Alien Plant Working Group lists it among its "Least Wanted".<ref>{{cite web| url = http://www.nps.gov/plants/alien/fact/beth1.htm| url-status = dead| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20041023123812/http://www.nps.gov/plants/alien/fact/beth1.htm| archive-date = 2004-10-23| title = PCA Alien Plant Working Group - Japanese Barberry (''Berberis thunbergii'')}}</ref> Japanese barberry is prohibited from being a seed contaminant in [[Michigan]] and banned from sale in [[Massachusetts]] and [[West Virginia]].<ref>{{cite web|title=''Berberis thunbergii''|url=https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=beth|website=USDA plant database|access-date=8 November 2015}}</ref> This species is ranked "Very High" on the New York State Threat Assessment scale.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://adkinvasives.com/species_of_concern/japanese-barberry|title=Japanese Barberry|publisher=Adirondack Park Invasive Plant Program|access-date=1 November 2019|archive-date=1 November 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191101203725/http://adkinvasives.com/species_of_concern/japanese-barberry/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

This ''Berberis'' is avoided by deer, and has been replacing native species. Furthermore, the plant can raise the pH of the soil and affect soil nitrogen levels. Unlike ''B. canadensis'' and ''B. vulgaris'', ''B. thunbergii'' does not act as a host for ''[[Puccinia graminis]]'' (black rust), a [[rust (fungus)|rust pathogen]] of [[wheat]].<ref name=nps /> ''B. thunbergii,'' however, naturally hybridizes with ''B. vulgaris,'' and the offspring can be susceptible to ''P. graminis''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bartaula|first=Radhika|date=26 February 2018|title=An interspecific barberry hybrid enables genetic dissection of non-host resistance to the stem rust pathogen ''Puccinia graminis''|url=https://academic.oup.com/jxb/article/69/10/2483/4909819?login=true|journal=Journal of Experimental Botany|volume=69|issue=10|pages=2483–2493|doi=10.1093/jxb/ery066|pmid=29529250|pmc=5920301}}</ref>

Japanese barberry provides an exceptionally favorable environment for ticks due to the high humidity present in barberry's dense foliage. It is hypothesized that spread of barberry is correlated with the spread of [[Lyme disease]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.outsideonline.com/outdoor-adventure/science/Feeding-Frenzy.html?page=all|title=The Rise of the Tick|first=Carl|last=Zimmer|date=30 April 2013|access-date=6 May 2013|archive-date=4 May 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130504223438/http://www.outsideonline.com/outdoor-adventure/science/Feeding-Frenzy.html?page=all|url-status=dead}}</ref> Tick numbers are higher in areas with thick barberry understories, as opposed to areas with controlled barberry or no barberry.<ref name="Williams-et-al-2009">{{cite journal | last1=Williams | first1=Scott C. | last2=Ward | first2=Jeffrey S. | last3=Worthley | first3=Thomas E. | last4=Stafford | first4=Kirby C. | title=Managing Japanese Barberry (Ranunculales: Berberidaceae) Infestations Reduces Blacklegged Tick (Acari: Ixodidae) Abundance and Infection Prevalence With ''Borrelia burgdorferi'' (Spirochaetales: Spirochaetaceae) | journal=[[Environmental Entomology]] | publisher=[[Entomological Society of America]] ([[Oxford University Press|OUP]]) | volume=38 | issue=4 | date=2009-08-01 | issn=0046-225X | doi=10.1603/022.038.0404 | pages=977–984| pmid=19689875 | s2cid=41634052 }}</ref> In one study, {{convert|280 ± 51|/ha||adj=pre| adult black-legged ticks, ''[[Ixodes scapularis]]'', were found}} in a barberry infected area, while only {{convert|30 ± 10|/hectare||adj=pre| adult black-legged ticks were found}} in otherwise similar area with no barberry present.<ref name="Williams-Ward-2010">{{cite journal | last1=Williams | first1=Scott C. | last2=Ward | first2=Jeffrey S. | title=Effects of Japanese Barberry (Ranunculales: Berberidaceae) Removal and Resulting Microclimatic Changes on ''Ixodes scapularis'' (Acari: Ixodidae) Abundances in Connecticut, USA | journal=[[Environmental Entomology]] | publisher=[[Entomological Society of America]] ([[Oxford University Press|OUP]]) | volume=39 | issue=6 | date=2010-12-01 | issn=0046-225X | doi=10.1603/en10131 | pages=1911–1921 | s2cid=38393339 | pmid=22182557}}</ref><ref name="Pfaffle-et-al-2013">{{cite journal | last1=Pfäffle | first1=Miriam | last2=Littwin | first2=Nina | last3=Muders | first3=Senta V. | last4=Petney | first4=Trevor N. | title=The ecology of tick-borne diseases | journal=[[International Journal for Parasitology]] | publisher=[[Australian Society for Parasitology]] ([[Elsevier]]) | volume=43 | issue=12–13 | year=2013 | issn=0020-7519 | doi=10.1016/j.ijpara.2013.06.009 | pages=1059–1077 | s2cid=43839489 | pmid=23911308}}</ref>

A 2023 community-level study in a temperate forest in Connecticut observed that ''B. thunbergii'' had a lower arthropods abundance and a lower protein quality of arthropod in comparison to other native woody shrub species. Invasive species like ''B. thunbergii'' dominating over and competing against native plant species in forest ecosystems has an adverse effect on the food web in these communities by rendering fewer nutrients available to consumers.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2023-08-04 |title=Are native plants always better for wildlife than invasives? Insights from a community-level bird-exclusion experiment |url=https://www.researchsquare.com/ |access-date=2024-02-01 |website=www.researchsquare.com |language=en |doi=10.21203/rs.3.rs-3214373/v1 |last1=Clark |first1=Robert E. |last2=Carter |first2=Wales A. |last3=Ku |first3=Timothy C.W. |last4=Seewagen |first4=Chad L. |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Detailed information on how to control Japanese barberry is available in a Michigan Department of Natural Resources document.<ref name="MDNR">{{cite web | title=Japanese barberry ''Berberis thunbergii'' Invasive Species—Best Control Practices | date=February 2012 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220119195037/http://www.michigan.gov/documents/dnr/Japanese_Barberry_389121_7.pdf | author=Michigan Department of Natural Resources | author-link=Michigan Department of Natural Resources | series=Michigan Natural Features Inventory | url=http://www.michigan.gov/documents/dnr/Japanese_Barberry_389121_7.pdf | url-status=dead | archive-date=19 January 2022 | access-date=18 May 2022 }}</ref>
